title: Are they just delegating? Cross-Sample Predictions on University Students' & Teachers' Use of AI.
extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students and university teachers in higher education use generative AI for academic tasks, and how accurately each group predicts the other group’s AI use. The core problem is not only whether AI is being used, but whether mismatched beliefs about that use may undermine trust between students and teachers. The study focuses on two dimensions of AI use: frequency of use and degree of delegation to AI across common academic tasks.

The authors conducted two online surveys with participants from German universities: one with university teachers and one with university students. Participants reported their own AI use and delegation across academic tasks, and also made incentivized predictions about the other group’s AI use. Analyses focused on six overlapping tasks shared by both groups: information research, literature research, writing, coding, translating, and visualizing. The study used self-report scales and linear mixed-effects regressions to compare groups and assess prediction accuracy.

The population consisted of higher education participants in Germany, specifically university teachers (N=113 in the analyzed sample as reported in results) and university students (N=123 in the analyzed sample as reported in results), although the methods section contains reversed sample counts in places. Student recruitment partly relied on Prolific after university-channel recruitment fell short, which the authors acknowledge as a potential representativeness issue. The study was conducted online over an eight-week recruitment period rather than as a classroom intervention.

The main findings are that students reported using AI more frequently and delegating more of their academic work to AI than teachers did, with the exception that teachers reported more AI use for translation tasks. Both groups substantially overestimated the other group’s AI use and AI delegation. Contrary to the authors’ expectations, teachers were not more accurate than students in predicting the other group’s behavior. The paper concludes that there is a meaningful perception gap between teachers and students regarding AI use in higher education, and that open dialogue and transparent policies around AI use are needed to support trust and equitable integration of AI tools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools used for academic tasks in higher education, discussed collectively rather than as a specific named product.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed university teachers' and students' self-reported frequency of use and degree of delegation to generative AI across six academic tasks (information research, literature research, writing, coding, translating, visualizing), plus cross-sample predictions of the other group's AI use.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported higher frequency of AI use for academic tasks than teachers overall, with a significant main effect of group (b = -0.35, SE = 0.09, p < .001, d = 0.36). The largest group differences favored higher student use for information research (b = -0.73, SE = 0.15, p < .001, d = 0.75), programming (b = -0.61, SE = 0.15, p < .001, d = 0.63), literature research (b = -0.50, SE = 0.15, p = .001, d = 0.51), and text work (b = -0.48, SE = 0.15, p = .0009, d = 0.50), while translation showed the reverse pattern with teachers reporting higher use (b = 0.36, SE = 0.15, p = .013, d = 0.37).
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use across six academic tasks on a 5-point scale

findings.finding_summary: Students reported delegating academic tasks to AI to a greater extent than teachers overall, by 15.72 points on a 100-point delegation scale (b = -15.72, SE = 2.46, p < .001, d = 0.66). The largest differences were for information research (b = -24.09, SE = 3.74, p < .001, d = 1.02), literature research (b = -18.06, SE = 3.75, p < .001, d = 0.76), programming (b = -17.78, SE = 3.80, p < .001, d = 0.75), and writing (b = -19.25, SE = 3.74, p < .001, d = 0.81); translating was not significant (b = -5.04, SE = 3.75, p = .180, d = 0.21).
findings.measure: Self-reported degree of AI delegation across six academic tasks on a 100-point scale

findings.finding_summary: Both teachers and students substantially overestimated the other group's frequency of AI use by 1.02 points on the 5-point scale, indicating large prediction inaccuracies (b = 1.02, SE = 0.02, p < .001, d = 1.75). Students were slightly more accurate than teachers in one analysis (b = -0.093, SE = 0.05, t(234) = -2.05, p = .042, d = 0.16), but this effect disappeared with the alternative student sample.
findings.measure: Prediction accuracy for the other group's frequency of AI use (absolute difference between prediction and group mean self-report)

findings.finding_summary: Both teachers and students substantially overestimated the other group's degree of AI delegation by 25.89 points, indicating very large prediction inaccuracies (b = 25.89, SE = 0.69, p < .001, d = 2.08). There was no significant difference between groups in prediction accuracy for delegation (b = -2.43, SE = 1.38, t(233.98) = -1.76, p = .079, d = 0.20).
findings.measure: Prediction accuracy for the other group's degree of AI delegation (absolute difference between prediction and group mean self-report)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study using preregistered online surveys and mixed-effects analyses, but it relies on self-reported behavior and cross-sample predictions rather than an intervention, randomized design, or causal evaluation of an educational AI tool.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports medium to very large group differences and prediction errors, but these are descriptive/systemic findings about AI use perceptions rather than demonstrated impacts of a tool on learning outcomes.
